subject: biology
title: Dominant and Recessive
welcome_lead: Learn how some features win the genetic battle while others hide in the background.
meta_desc: KS3 Biology adventure introducing dominant and recessive features.
final_note: You can now explain dominant and recessive features with everyday examples.

concepts.def: Allele that always shows if present.

How features pass from parents to children.

walkthroughs.body_html: You inherit two copies of every gene — one from each parent. These versions are called alleles and can be the same or different.
A dominant allele always shows its effect if at least one copy is present. Brown eye colour is often a dominant feature.
A recessive allele only shows its effect if both copies are recessive. Blue eyes can be a recessive trait — parents may both carry the allele without showing it.

options: Arteries and veins both carry the same mixed blood through the body.
Transpiration pull — evaporation from leaves creates tension that pulls water up the continuous water column.

mcqs.q: Why is the cohesion-tension theory critical for water transport in plants?
options: Hydrogen bonds between water molecules keep the water column unbroken under tension, so transpiration can pull water up from the roots.
Capillary action alone is enough to lift water to the top of any tree.
Cohesion-tension describes how water diffuses freely between cells.
Cohesion-tension explains how plants store water in the xylem like a reservoir.

mcqs.q: Do all arteries carry oxygenated blood?
options: Arteries and veins both carry the same mixed blood through the body.
Capillary action alone is enough to lift water to the top of any tree.
No — the pulmonary artery carries deoxygenated blood from the heart to the lungs.
All arteries carry oxygenated blood and all veins carry deoxygenated blood.
